first_design.spec_text:
ADDED [OBJ-6] (§VIII.1, after [OBJ-5]) **One value, one place.**
- Where a value lives is decided once, where it is made: inside its owner (a frame, or the struct or list that holds it) or in a block of its own. For a block, the decision includes which header of [OBJ-1] it has and which memory manager it comes from ([ALC-1]). For a static, it includes read-only or writable memory ([CT-5]).
- The compiler decides this from every line of the program that may use the value, never from the line at hand alone. It follows the value through hand-overs, returns, calls (by their summaries, [BCK-8]), fields and elements, as it follows views and stored functions.
- The program's words say what kind of value it is: held alone, `owns`, a class object, or shared by `shares`, `shares mut` or `thread_shared`. The compiler decides only when its block is made and which header it has. It makes no block that no word or type asks for.
- From where it is made, the value keeps its address and its header for as long as anything points at it: a view, an owner, a `weakref` or `sharedref mut` link, or an address C keeps ([FFI-35a]).
- A value moves only at these lines, and each first ends what points at the old place:
  - a hand-over (`b = a`, an `owns` argument, `return a`), which ends the giver's views ([BCK-4]);
  - a reshape of a holder that stores the value inline (`push`, `insert`), which ends views and links into its inline elements (verdict 81, [BRW-17]);
  - a hand-over to another thread of an object a `weakref` link on this thread points at. Its old block stays here marked ended, and for an object C keeps the line stops the program ([THR-2], verdict 114);
  - a reload ([HR-12]).
- Every other line finds the value already where that line needs it: a line that shares the value, makes a link or an owner of it, or gives C its address.
- Where nothing could tell the difference, the compiler may instead make the value in its owner and move it at that line, so that a path that never reaches the line makes no block. "Nothing could tell" means no view, owner, link or address of the value is live across that line. The move is one copy of the value's bytes, as `std::make_shared<T>(std::move(v))` does.
- Nothing is checked while the program runs for any of this.

CHANGED [HEAP-3]: "any other value is put in a block where it is made shared (...), one allocation" becomes:
"any other value is put in one block of its own, made where the value is made, or at the line that shares it where nothing points into it across that line ([OBJ-6]) (`count = shares mut Counter()`, `other = shares items`): one allocation either way."

CHANGED [RC-1]: after "Only a whole value is shared (verdict 103):" the sentence becomes:
"`shares x`, `shares mut x` and `thread_shared x` are written before a new value, a whole value this function owns (a local; an `owns` parameter is one), a static ([STA-1]), or a name that is already such an owner. The value is then one value under all its names: every view, link and address made of it before the line points at it after the line ([OBJ-6]). A place that has one owner and is not a local of this function or a static is `E2122`, as now (a list element, a field, a plain parameter; message unchanged)."

Added to [RC-1]:
- "After `thread_shared x`, `x` is one of the value's owners on any thread and does only what such an owner does. It reads the value, and changes it only through an `Atomic`, a lock, a channel or a `guarded by` field (`E7014`, [RC-7]): "`s` is shared between threads (line 10), so no owner changes it directly, and line 14 sets its port; set it before line 10, or make the field `port: Atomic[int]`"."
- "A name made of the value before that line that may change it directly (a `shares mut` owner, a `sharedref mut` link), and is used after the line, is `E7014` at that use. Where that use is in another function, it is `E7014` at the sharing line."
- "What is reachable from the value is checked at the line that makes it `thread_shared` (`E7015`, verdict 165)."
- "A static never ends, so no owner made of it ends it. `shares mut` of a static is `E3023` (a static never changes)."

CHANGED [THR-1]: "it is written before a new value (`st = thread_shared Stats()`) or on a value already `thread_shared` (`fn() thread_shared st:`), and on a value made otherwise it is `E7017` (...)" becomes:
"it is written where `shares x` may be ([RC-1]): before a new value (`st = thread_shared Stats()`), a local of this function (`shared = thread_shared s` after `s` is filled in), a static, or a value already `thread_shared` (`fn() thread_shared st:`)."

CHANGED [OWN-13]: "`thread_shared x` ... written only before a new value (...) or a value already `thread_shared` (`E7017` otherwise: ...)" becomes:
"`thread_shared x`, one more owner on any thread, written where `shares x` may be ([RC-1], `E2122`)."

CHANGED code table ([XVII]):
- `E7017` is retired ("no longer given: `thread_shared` follows a local as `shares` does, [RC-1]").
- `E2122` reads "made of a place that has one owner and is not a local of this function or a static (a list element, a field, a plain parameter)".
- `E2119` adds "or of a value held alone in its owner (a struct local)".

CHANGED [OBJ-1], added: "A value that some line may make `thread_shared` has that header from where it is made, including a local shared after it is made ([OBJ-6])."

CHANGED [RC-4] point 4, added: "`thread_shared x` of a value that may have reached this thread held alone from another thread (through a channel, a spawn's capture, a job) marks it handed over at that line, so all its owners count in the away count."

CHANGED [BCK-4], added: "Sharing a value, and making an owner or a link of it, is not a storage end: its views live on ([OBJ-6])."

CHANGED [CT-5], first bullet:
"in a `static` (not `static mut`) whose memory no line of the program writes, the value is materialised in read-only memory. A write here means a field changed through a `Mutex`, `RwLock`, `Cell`, `Atomic`, a `guarded by` field, or any type changed through a read-only name, or a count in its header written by an owner or a `weakref` link made of it. A static whose header alone is written is materialised the same way, in writable memory, with no initialisation code. Statics are never dropped, so no count ends them;"

CHANGED [WK-11], added:
- "A link or an owner made of a static by its name counts on the main thread, which holds the module's variables ([THR-20]).
- Made, ended or opened in a function that may run on another thread, it is `E7015` ([THR-2]): "`ORIGIN` counts its links on the main thread without atomics, and `follow_origin` runs on the thread started on line 14; make the link on the main thread, or share the static between threads: `static ORIGIN: thread_shared Node = thread_shared Node()`".
- A static declared `thread_shared`, or one that some line makes `thread_shared`, counts for several threads for its whole life ([RC-4])."

CHANGED [HEAP-7], added: "A `weakref` of a value held alone in its owner (a struct local, which a hand-over moves) is `E2119` as for a part ([WK-16]): make it shared (`inv = shares Inventory(...)`) or a class."

CHANGED [CORO-6], first sentence:
"A view into the generator's own frame (a view of one of its own locals) may be held across a `yield`.
- The frame then stays where it is while that view is held ([OBJ-6]). The compiler makes it where it is kept: a local, or the block of an `owns` place it is handed to (`sched.add(owns walk(route))`).
- A line that would move the suspended frame into a place that stores it inline (an element of a list of frames, a field) while such a view is held is `E2221` at that line: "`g` holds a view into its own frame (`r`, line 3) while it is suspended, and line 12 moves it into `gens`, which stores frames inline; keep each in a block of its own: `gens: Array[owns dyn Iterator[Item = int]]` and `gens.push(owns g)`"."
The rest of [CORO-6] is unchanged (a `for` over its own list walks by position). [CORO-5] holds as written: no block is added that the program did not write.

UNCHANGED: verdict 103's refusals (`E2122` for an element, a field, a plain parameter), [WK-16], [RC-7], [THR-2]'s hand-over (verdict 114), [FFI-35a].

answers.answer:
Sharing a local does not end its storage (BCK-4, as added). `inv` is one value under all its names.

The compiler sees that line 11 shares `inv` and that `g` (line 10) is used on line 12, after it. So it makes `inv` in its shared block on line 9: the same one allocation line 11 needs, two lines earlier, with no copy at line 11. `g` points into a block that never moves.

This is draft option B, stated for every kind of pointer (a view, a link, an owner, an address C keeps), not only for views.
answers.code:
struct Inventory:
    gold: int
    items: Array[String]

class Shop:
    stock: shares mut Inventory

fn main():
    inv = Inventory(gold=5, items=[String("sword")])   # made in its shared block: line 11 shares it
    g = ref inv.gold                                    # points into that block
    shop = Shop(stock=shares mut inv)                   # one more owner; nothing moves
    println(g)                                          # 5
    inv.gold += 1                                       # inv keeps what it could do (verdict 23)
    println(shop.stock.gold)                            # 6
answers.outcome:
Compiles and prints 5, then 6.

If `inv.gold += 1` is written above `println(g)`, it stays E3021: a change while `g` reads the field (BRW-1), exactly as without sharing.

Without line 10, nothing points into `inv` across line 11. The compiler may then keep `inv` in `main`'s frame and move it into the block at line 11 (one copy of its bytes), so a path that never shares makes no block. Nothing runs while the program runs for either choice.

answers.answer:
`thread_shared` follows a local the way `shares` and `shares mut` do (RC-1). Draft option B, the phase-3 recommendation.

The compiler sees line 10, so `s` is made on line 8 with the 32-byte thread_shared header. Until line 10 its home count counts `main`'s one owner with the same plain adds a one-thread object uses. Line 10 adds one more owner.

From line 10 on, `s` does what any owner of a thread_shared value does: it reads the value, and changes it only through an Atomic, a lock, a channel or a guarded field (E7014). E7015 checks at line 10 that a Settings is Send and ThreadShared (verdict 165).

No other Settings object gets the bigger header, and nothing moves. The cost that draft A gave as its reason does not arise, because the compiler sees both lines.
answers.code:
import std.thread

class Settings:
    port: int = 0
    verbose: bool = false

fn main():
    s = Settings()                      # made with the shared header: line 10 shares it between threads
    s.port = 8080                       # main is its only owner: a plain write
    shared = thread_shared s            # one more owner, on any thread; E7015 checks Settings here
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() thread_shared shared: println(shared.port))
    h.join()                            # 8080
    println(s.port)                     # s still reads it: 8080
answers.outcome:
Compiles and prints 8080 twice.

Adding `s.port = 9` as line 14 is E7014: "`s` is shared between threads (line 10), so no owner changes it directly, and line 14 sets its port; set it before line 10, or make the field `port: Atomic[int]`".

A `shares mut` owner or a `sharedref mut` link made of `s` before line 10 and used to change it afterwards is E7014 as well.

The contradiction is resolved in RC-1's direction. RC-1's sentence stands for all three sharing words. THR-1, OWN-13 and E7017's row take RC-1's wording, and E7017 is retired.

J7-05's lead-fix text, which would narrow RC-1, is not written.

What E7017 rested on, for the owner: the redesign's rule R3 (run 3, fix F-08), not a verdict. Its reason was that "it would freeze a value that its own line lets its owner change". Under the rule a later line narrows what `names` may do, as a hand-over (`t = owns names`) already does. The word is on that line, and E7014's message names it. Option C keeps R3.
answers.code:
import std.thread

class Names:
    items: Array[String] = []

fn share_and_keep(owns first: String):
    names = Names()
    names.items.push(owns first)                  # filled while this function is its only owner
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() thread_shared names: names.items.len())
    println(names.items.len(), h.join())          # 1 1
answers.outcome:
Compiles and prints `1 1`. THR-1's own E7017 example becomes a program that compiles.

`names.items.push(...)` after line 9 is E7014: "`names` is shared between threads (line 9), so no owner changes it directly, and line 10 pushes to its list; push before line 9". The capture word means exactly what it means before a value (OWN-13, CLO-2).

answers.answer:
Making a link writes the static's header, so by CT-5 (as changed) ORIGIN is placed in writable memory. It is still built when compiling, with no initialisation code. Its weak count starts at 1 for its owner, the static, which never ends, so the count never reaches 0.

The link is counted like any one-thread object's, on the main thread, which holds the module's variables (THR-20). A link made, ended or opened on another thread is E7015, as THR-2 already says for every one-thread target. A static declared `thread_shared` may be linked from any thread.

This is draft option A, with the thread named.
answers.outcome:
Compiles and prints 0.0 0.0. Nothing runs that would not run for any other link: one plain add and one compare (WK-11).

Called on a spawned thread (`h = thread.spawn(owns fn(): spot())`, where `spot` makes its own Camera and calls `follow_origin`), the link line is E7015: "`ORIGIN` counts its links on the main thread without atomics, and `follow_origin` runs on the thread started on line 14; make the link on the main thread, or share the static between threads: `static ORIGIN: thread_shared Node = thread_shared Node()`". Written that way, it compiles.

other_cases.case: `weakref` of a local (WK-11: any name may make a link)
other_cases.settled:
Allowed for a class object local, which already lives in its block (its weak count is decided by class family, OBJ-1), and for a local made shared.

A plain struct local held alone is E2119, as a part is: no word asks for a block, and the rule adds none. A hand-over would move the struct under the link. Help: `inv = shares Inventory(...)`, or make it a class.

other_cases.case: `into_raw()` of a local, or a local object given to C under a `retained` contract (verdict 114, fix 3)
other_cases.settled:
The object keeps its address for as long as C keeps it (OBJ-6). If a later line makes it `thread_shared`, the compiler has already given it the 32-byte header where it was made, because it sees both lines. So C's address stays right and nothing moves.

The one move that would be needed, verdict 114's hand-over to another thread while a link here points at the object, stops the program at that line, as fix 3 says. Which owner keeps such an object alive is P08's question.

other_cases.case: `shares ORIGIN`, `shares mut ORIGIN` and `thread_shared ORIGIN` of a static's object
other_cases.settled:
`shares ORIGIN` is allowed, on the main thread. Verdict 103's reason is untrue for a static, as it is for a local: the compiler sees every line that shares that one value, and a static never ends, so no end anywhere tests a count. ORIGIN goes to writable memory, and its count never reaches 0.

`shares mut ORIGIN` is E3023, because a static never changes.

An owner or link made on another thread is E7015, unless the static is `thread_shared`. A static that some line makes `thread_shared` gets the 32-byte header and counts for several threads for its whole life, since a static has no 'before'. This widens RC-1's text, not verdict 103's words, so it is part of this question.

other_cases.case: A link or view into an inline struct element of a list, then a `push` (verdict 81)
other_cases.settled:
A push that moves inline elements is one of OBJ-6's moves. It ends views and links into them first: E3060 at a later use. The compiler never boxes a list's elements, because the list's layout is its type's (verdict 103's layout reason).

A position view (`boss = ref mut enemies[0]`) is found again after the push (BCK-6). A view or link of a class object in the list is not ended (verdict 81).

other_cases.case: An object handed to another thread while a `weakref` link here points at it (verdict 114)
A reload that changes a type's layout (P09)
other_cases.settled: A reload is OBJ-6's fourth move. P09's rule must carry every live value to the new layout so that, afterwards, no view, link, owner or C address points at an old place unless that place is marked ended. A reload that adds a new `thread_shared` line for objects already made with a small header is a header change that P09's migration carries.

other_cases.case: A local captured by a function that outlives its maker (verdict 80)
other_cases.settled:
`fn() owns n:` is a hand-over. It ends the maker's views of `n` (BCK-4), and `n` moves into the function's state block, which is made where the function value is made.

The compiler never moves a captured local by itself or shares it with the maker, because verdict 80 keeps that meaning written. OBJ-6 decides only where storage the words already ask for is put.

other_cases.case: A generator holding a view of its own local across `yield` (CORO-6, E2221 today)
A class object taken out of a list (`j = queue.jobs.pop()`), then `shared = thread_shared j`
other_cases.settled:
The compiler follows the value back, per field, to the lines that make objects that may enter `Queue.jobs`, and gives those objects the 32-byte header.

Where no `weakref` link anywhere in the program can name that class and C keeps no address of the object, nothing can point at it at the sharing line. The compiler may then move it there instead: one allocation, one copy and one free, as Rust's `Arc::from(Box)` does. Either way no pointer sees a move, and nothing is refused.

other_cases.case: A value handed whole to this thread from another thread, then made `thread_shared` here
other_cases.settled: Its block came from the other thread's memory chunk, which is where OBJ-1 reads the maker from. So the sharing line marks the value handed over (RC-4 point 4, verdict 101 fix 2): one atomic add, after which every owner counts in the away count. The count this thread kept while it held the value alone is never left behind.

other_cases.case: Sharing on one path only, with a view crossing the sharing line (`g = ref inv.gold`, `if rare: shop = Shop(stock=shares mut inv)`, `println(g)`)
other_cases.settled:
The block is made at `inv`'s line on every path. That is one allocation on a path that never shares, which a C program keeping a stable pointer into the struct would also pay with an up-front `malloc`.

With no crossing view, the block is made only on the path that shares.

other_cases.case: A `shares mut` owner or `sharedref mut` link made of `s`, then `thread_shared s`
other_cases.settled:
A change through that owner or link after the sharing line is E7014 at the change, because no name changes a value shared between threads directly. If the owner escaped into a field that some other function uses to change it, the error is E7014 at the sharing line, naming the field. A field that is never used to change the value is accepted.

A `ref mut` view of `s` live across the line is E3021 (BRW-1).

other_cases.case: A local made with `using arena`, then shared
other_cases.settled: Its block comes from the manager its making line names (ALC-1), made there once. Whether a `thread_shared` value may live in a manager is P02's J5-05, and that rule applies at the sharing line unchanged.

other_cases.case: A `static mut` object that a `weakref` link points at
other_cases.settled: It is already in writable memory, built on first access (STA-3). Its links count on the main thread, which holds it (THR-20). A link made from another thread is E7015 (THR-2), and a static mut reached from another thread without its lock is E7012, as now.

first_design.prior_art:
Go: escape analysis decides, when compiling, whether a variable lives on the stack or the heap, from every use including callees (through escape tags on parameters). So `p := &x.f; share(&x)` keeps `p` valid ("moved to heap: x"). This is J5-06 B's mechanism. Go pays a garbage collector to free those blocks. Ember takes the analysis without the collector.

Rust:
- `Rc::new(inv)` and `Arc::new(s)` move the value, and a borrow across the move is refused (E0505). That is option B: correct programs refused.
- `Arc::from(Box<T>)` reallocates and copies.
- `Weak` needs an `Rc` or `Arc`, so there is no weak link to a static.
- A `static` goes to read-only memory unless its type contains an `UnsafeCell` (the `Freeze` property). That is a property, where CT-5 has a list.
- A self-borrow across `yield` or `await` needs `Pin`, or `Box::pin` (a written word, plus an allocation).

C++:
- `int& g = inv.gold; auto sp = std::make_shared<Inventory>(std::move(inv));` leaves `g` on the moved-from local: undefined behaviour, with no diagnostic.
- `std::shared_ptr<T>(std::move(unique))` avoids the move with a separate control block. That costs two allocations, a two-word owner and atomic counts always.
- `enable_shared_from_this` requires the object to be created shared.
- C++20 coroutines heap-allocate every frame unless the optimiser elides it.

Swift: every class object carries a 16-byte header with atomic counts from birth, so it pays always. Globals are initialised lazily. A statically initialised global object is marked immortal, and retain and release test that mark while running. CPython 3.12 does the same (PEP 683: a branch on every incref and decref).

C#: the garbage collector moves objects and rewrites every reference; `fixed` pins an object for C.

Ada: a local whose address is taken must be declared `aliased` (a written storage word).

Zig: nothing is checked; a pointer to a moved stack value dangles.

Where each falls short of safe, as fast as C and readable:
- C++ and Zig: not safe.
- Rust: refuses the correct program, and needs `Pin` ceremony.
- Swift, Go and C#: pay at run time on every object (atomic counts, a collector).
- Ada: the programmer writes the fact.

OBJ-6 combines Go's compile-time placement, Rust's checks and C++'s cost, with nothing checked while the program runs.
first_design.cost:
Per operation, against C:

Sharing a local struct (`shares`, `shares mut`, `thread_shared`):
- One allocation, the same as today.
- Where a view crosses the sharing line, the block is made at the local's line and the value is built in it. That saves today's copy of its bytes at the sharing line.
- Otherwise the compiler may move it at the sharing line: one copy of its bytes, as C++'s `make_shared(std::move(inv))` and Rust's `Rc::new(inv)`.
- Field access before the share goes through the block's address, as in C with a `malloc`ed struct.
- Zero run-time checks.

`thread_shared s` of a class object made in the function:
- The 32-byte header from its making line: 20 bytes more than a 12-byte header (24 more than 8), exactly what `thread_shared Settings()` costs today.
- Until the sharing line every count operation is the same plain add on the home count that a one-thread object does: zero difference.
- The sharing line is one plain add (one more owner on the making thread). It adds one atomic add only when the value may have come from another thread (RC-4 point 4).
- C++'s `make_shared` pays a 16-byte control block with atomic counts on every owner copy. Rust's `Arc::new` pays 16 bytes, atomic counts and a move.

A class object reaching a sharing line from a list or a field:
- The bigger header on every object the compiler cannot tell apart from it (the making lines whose objects may enter that field). That is the granularity at which OBJ-1 already pays the weak count, per class family.
- Where no link can name the class and C keeps no address of the object, the compiler may move it instead: one allocation, one copy and one free, as Rust's `Arc::from(Box)`.

A link or a `shares` owner of a static:
- Zero run-time cost: the static's bytes move from read-only data to writable data, the same size, still with no initialisation code.
- A link costs what every link costs: one plain add and one compare (WK-11).

A view across `yield` in a generator:
- Zero: no block is added.
- A frame handed to an `owns` place gets that block where it is made instead of at the hand-over: the same one allocation, made earlier.

When compiling: following values through calls, fields and elements, which the compiler already does for views, stored functions (by field) and weakref classes.

Nothing is checked or counted while the program runs that a program sharing the same values does not already pay.

readability.note:
No new word, attribute or ceremony. The program after the rule is shorter: it needs no helper function to build a value before sharing it between threads.

In J5-06's shop program, the view is taken where the program needs it instead of being moved below the sharing line. A game loop or parser that shares nothing reads and compiles exactly as before.

The only lines that read differently are refusals, and each names the sharing line: E7014's "set it before line 10".

first_design.misuse:
Refused when compiling:
- A direct change of `s` after `thread_shared s`: E7014, naming the sharing line, with "set it before line 10, or make the field Atomic".
- A `shares mut` owner or `sharedref mut` link made of `s` before that line and used to change it after: E7014 at the change, or at the sharing line when the change is in another function.
- A `ref mut` view of `s` live across the line: E3021 (BRW-1).
- Something reachable from `s` that is not Send and ThreadShared: E7015 at the sharing line (verdict 165).
- A change of `inv` while a view taken before the sharing line is still used: E3021, exactly as without sharing.
- Sharing a part of a one-owner place (an element, a field, a plain parameter): E2122 (verdict 103).
- `weakref` of a struct local: E2119, "make it shared".
- `shares mut` of a static: E3023.
- A link or owner of a one-thread static made, ended or opened on another thread: E7015, giving `static ORIGIN: thread_shared Node = thread_shared Node()`.
- Moving a suspended generator frame that holds a view into itself into inline storage: E2221 at that line, giving the `owns` spelling.

Stopped at the line while running, unchanged: a hand-over to another thread of an object C keeps while a weakref here points at it (verdict 114, fix 3), with its existing message.

Under the rule, no view, link, owner or C address ever outlives the place its value occupies, except through a line that first ends it (a hand-over, a reshape, verdict 114's move, a reload). So no program the rule allows reads a moved-from or freed place, races, or has undefined behaviour.

A forgotten word cannot cause a crash: leaving out `thread_shared` leaves a one-thread value, and the cross-thread lines are refused (E7015).
first_design.verdicts:
23 (the first owner keeps what it could do after sharing; a local may be shared): kept.
- `shares` and `shares mut` of a local work as now, and their views now survive.
- For `thread_shared`, the first owner keeps what any owner of a value shared between threads may do. That is verdict 23's own last clause ("that is thread_shared, through a lock") and RC-7's "A thread_shared value is never changed directly by any owner".

- The header is chosen where the value is made.
- The maker is the thread whose chunk the block came from.
- Sharing a value that came from another thread uses fix 2's step.

103 (shares is not made from a one-owner place: an element, a field, a plain parameter): kept, with its reason.

- For a local shared later, the line that makes it thread_shared is `thread_shared s`, and E7015 is reported there.
- It is not reported at `s = Settings()`, whose line says nothing about threads. Choice (a) over (b) stands.

80 (what a function keeps when it outlives its maker is written, `owns n`, over the compiler moving it in itself): kept. OBJ-6 decides only where storage the words already ask for goes, never who owns a value.

Under A a later line narrows what `s` may do, as a hand-over already does: the word is on that line, and E7014 names it. Option C keeps R3 for the owner to choose.

first_design.open_risks:
1. Header sizes and field offsets (not created here). OBJ-2 says an owner or view points at offset 0, while OBJ-1's headers are 8, 12 or 32 bytes, so a class's fields sit at different offsets in a one-thread object and a `thread_shared` one. The spec does not say how one compiled function reads both. It is already needed today: a method runs on `Stats()` and on `thread_shared Stats()`. Option A makes 32-byte objects of ordinary classes more common. A representation rule is needed, for example the one-thread fields at fixed offsets from the value.

2. A link place that may hold both kinds of target. A `weakref` field that may hold a link to a one-thread object and to a `thread_shared` one needs one way to open it (WK-12 differs for the two). The spec is silent today. Under A, an object linked before it was shared makes this more common.

3. Whole-program header choice is an over-approximation. For class objects arriving through a list or a field, objects that are never shared may carry 20 extra bytes. This should be measured on a real program (a job queue, an ECS) before the bound is claimed to the owner. The fallback, moving the object where nothing can point at it, covers classes no `weakref` names.

4. The statics' home thread. "The main thread" in WK-11's added sentence must follow P01's J8-10 (main or creator under exports).

5. A `thread_shared` static's home count. Such a static comes from no thread's memory chunk, while OBJ-1 reads the maker from the chunk. Its image section needs a chunk header naming the main thread, or a proof that RC-4's queue is never reached for a value that never ends. This is implementation, but the runtime must state it.

6. Escaped owners. E7014 at the sharing line for a `shares mut` owner that escaped into a field depends on following that owner per field. Where the compiler cannot tell, it refuses at the sharing line, which may refuse a correct program that never uses that field to change the value.

7. R3's readability reason is the owner's to weigh: a later line narrows what `s` may do. Option C exists for it.

8. P09 (reload) and P02 (managers, J5-05) must state their halves. A reload carries header changes. A block made early comes from the manager the making line names, and J5-05 may refuse `thread_shared` there.

9. Out-of-memory stops can move earlier. When a view crosses the sharing line, a stop for lack of memory happens at the making line instead of the sharing line. It stays in the same function, so effects do not move.

10. The CORO-6 change accepts programs that E2221 refuses today. The compiler must know every line that may move a suspended frame. A test set for frames in lists, fields and returns is needed.

ADDED [OBJ-6] (§VIII.1, after [OBJ-5]) **One value, one place.**
- A value lives in one place, and the type of every holder says what kind of place it is:
  - a value held alone (`T`, `owns T`): inline in its owner, or, for a class object or an `owns` value, a block of its own with the one-thread header of [OBJ-1];
  - a value held `shares` or `shares mut`: a block with the one-thread header;
  - a value held `thread_shared`: a block with the header of [RC-4] ([OBJ-1]).
  So the code for any holder (its reads, its count operations, its end) follows from its type, in every package and in every function compiled once.
- A sharing line changes what the name it is written on is. From `shares x`, `shares mut x` or `thread_shared x` (a capture list's word included, [CLO-2]), the local `x` is one of the value's owners, of the type the word gives: `shares mut T` (`shares T` where `x` only read it) or `thread_shared T`.
  - It is that owner also after any point where a path through the line meets a path around it. A block's count holds its one owner (1), so its end is right on both paths.
  - A hand-over of `x` hands that owner over ([RC-2d]), and a place that holds the value alone does not take it (`E2020`): "`p` is one of the player's owners since line 9 (`roster.push(shares p)`), and `captain` would hold it alone and end it while `roster` still owns it; write `captain: shares mut Player` in `Team` (line 5), and `Team(captain=shares mut p)` on line 12".
- The function that shares a value gives it that place from where its storage begins in the function. So a view, a raw address or an address C keeps, taken before the sharing line, points into the place the line needs:
  - a struct, an enum or another inline value: its block, from where the function first gives it storage, whatever fills it (a literal, a call's result, an element taken out of a list, an `owns` parameter);
  - a class object a line of the function makes: the header the sharing line needs, from that line;
  - a class object that reaches the function from elsewhere (a parameter, a call's result, an element taken out of a list) and that the function makes `thread_shared`: it is moved into a block with that header where it reaches the function, by verdict 114's step ([THR-2]):
    - one compare of its weak count;
    - with no link, the old block is freed;
    - with a link, the old block stays on this thread marked ended, so every link here finds it ended;
    - an object C keeps ([FFI-35a]) never moves, so that line stops the program.
  - The compiler may instead make the block, or do the move, at the sharing line where nothing could tell the difference: no later use or end of the value is reached both by a path through that line and by one around it, and no view, address or other name of the value is live across it. A raw address taken of the value or of a part of it counts as live for the rest of the value's life. A path that never shares then makes no block.
- The block comes from the memory manager the sharing line names ([ALC-1]). Where that instance is made after the value's storage begins, the block is made at the sharing line instead. That ends the views of the value taken before the line ([BCK-4], `E3060`): "`shares mut inv using level` (line 11) puts `inv` in a block of `level`, made on line 10, after `inv` (line 8), and `g` views `inv` from line 9 and is used on line 12; take `g` after line 11, or make `level` above line 8".
- Every `weakref` link to a value shared between threads is made through a `thread_shared` name, because its weak count is atomic ([RC-4]). A link made through another name is `E7015` at the line that makes it:
  - in a function that may make the value `thread_shared`: through any other name of it, on any path;
  - for any value shared between threads: at a call that may make a link of it through a plain parameter (by the callee's summary, [BCK-8]).
  Message: "`panel.shown` (line 17) links to `s` through `s`, whose links count without atomics, and line 19 shares `s` between threads; make the link from the shared owner after line 19: `panel.shown = weakref shared`".
- A value moves only at these lines, and each first ends what points at the old place:
  - a hand-over of a value held alone (`b = a`, an `owns` argument, `return a`), which ends the giver's views ([BCK-4]);
  - a reshape of a holder that stores the value inline (`push`, `insert`), which ends views and links into its inline elements (verdict 81, [BRW-17]);
  - a move of a class object to another thread (verdict 114, [THR-2]) or into a block shared between threads (above). It leaves this thread's links on the old block, marked ended, and stops the program for an object C keeps;
  - a reload ([HR-15]).
  A raw pointer is not used after any of these ([UNS-4]).
- A generator's frame is a value like any other. A hand-over or a reshape moves it, and no move can end a view that the frame holds into itself, so such a view is not held across a `yield` ([CORO-6], unchanged).
- Nothing is checked while the program runs for any of this, except verdict 114's one compare where a class object that a `weakref` may name is moved.

Go: escape analysis decides, when compiling and per function (with escape tags on callees' parameters), whether a variable lives on the stack or the heap. So `p := &x.f; share(&x)` keeps `p` valid ("moved to heap: x"). That is OBJ-6's placement: decided in one function from its own lines and its callees' summaries. Go frees those blocks with a garbage collector; Ember frees them by count.

Rust:
- `Rc` and `Arc` are different types, so every holder's type states its counting protocol. That is what the type a sharing line gives a name does here.
- `Rc::new(inv)` and `Arc::new(s)` move the value, and a borrow across the move is refused (E0505). That is option B: correct programs refused.
- An `Rc` becomes an `Arc` by `Arc::new(Rc::try_unwrap(rc)?)`: a move, after which every `Weak` fails to upgrade. That is verdict 114's step, used here for a class object that reaches a function from elsewhere. `Arc::from(Box<T>)` allocates and copies, as that move does.
- A `static` goes to read-only memory unless its type has interior mutability (`Freeze`): a property of the type, as CT-5's addition here is.
- `Weak` needs an `Rc` or `Arc`, so Rust has no weak link to a static.
- A view into a generator's own frame across `yield` needs `Pin`. Ember refuses it (CORO-6, unchanged).

C++:
- `int& g = inv.gold; auto sp = std::make_shared<Inventory>(std::move(inv));` leaves `g` pointing at the moved-from local: undefined behaviour, with no diagnostic.
- `make_shared` puts a 16-byte control block with atomic counts before the object, always.
- `shared_ptr<T>(std::move(unique))` adds a second allocation.

Swift: every class object carries a 16-byte header with atomic counts from birth. Globals are initialised lazily. Statically initialised objects are treated as immortal, and retain and release test for that while running. CPython 3.12 does the same (PEP 683: a branch on every incref and decref).

Objective-C's non-fragile ABI reads instance-variable offsets from a variable at run time, so a class's layout can change beneath it. Here only the two counting words after a `thread_shared` value are found that way, and only when the exact type is not known when compiling.

Ada: a local whose address is taken is declared `aliased`.

Zig: nothing is checked; a pointer to a moved stack value dangles.

Where each falls short of safe, as fast as C and readable:
- C++ and Zig are not safe.
- Rust refuses the correct program and needs `Pin`.
- Swift, Go and CPython pay at run time on every object.
- Ada makes the programmer write the fact.

OBJ-6 takes Go's per-function placement, Rust's typed protocols and verdict 114's run-time step. Nothing is checked while the program runs except that one compare.
method1_repair.cost:
Per operation, against C:

Sharing a struct (`shares`, `shares mut`, `thread_shared`):
- One allocation, the same as today.
- Where something points into the struct across the sharing line, the block is made where the struct's storage begins and the value is built in it. That removes today's copy at the sharing line.
- Otherwise the compiler may make the block at the sharing line: one copy of its bytes, as C++'s `make_shared(std::move(inv))` and Rust's `Rc::new(inv)`. A path that never shares then allocates nothing.
- Field access before the share goes through the block's address, as in C with a `malloc`ed struct.
- Zero run-time checks.

`thread_shared` of a class object the function makes:
- 16 bytes more from its making line: exactly verdict 101's figure, and what `thread_shared Settings()` costs.
- Zero copies.
- Until the sharing line nothing is counted (the object is held alone). The line itself is one plain add on the home count.
- C++'s `make_shared` pays a 16-byte control block with atomic counts on every owner copy. Rust's `Arc::new` pays 16 bytes, atomic counts and a move.

The layout:
- The making thread's plain count operations stay at offset 0, as now.
- An away-count operation (another thread's owner, a queue step) through an owner whose exact type is not known when compiling (a base class, `dyn`) reads the value's size from its type information. That is two loads beside the atomic it guards.
- For a struct or a final class, the offset is a constant.
- Every `thread_shared` value is 4 to 8 bytes smaller than in today's 32-byte table.

`thread_shared` of a class object that reaches the function from elsewhere (a parameter, a call's result, an element taken out of a list):
- One allocation, one copy of its fields and one free, made where it reaches the function or at the sharing line. This is Rust's `Arc::from(Box)`.
- One compare of its weak count where a `weakref` may name its class (verdict 114's).
- No other object of its class pays anything.
- Today's `thread_shared build_settings()` pays the same.

A link to a static's object:
- Zero at run time. The object's bytes move from read-only data to writable data, the same size, still with no initialisation code.
- A link costs what every link costs: one plain add and one compare (WK-11).
- A `thread_shared` static's counts are atomic, as for any value shared between threads.

The owner type from the sharing line, E7015 for links, E7017, E2020 and the summary fact are all compile time.

Nothing is checked or counted while the program runs that a program sharing the same values does not already pay. The one exception is verdict 114's compare, where a class object a `weakref` may name is moved.

owner_short.today:
Sharing a local is allowed, but its block is made at the sharing line, so an earlier view reads where the local used to be. After sharing, the local can still be handed into a place that frees it alone.

`thread_shared` of a local is both allowed (RC-1) and refused (THR-1, E7017, which comes from the redesign's rule R3, not a verdict).

A `weakref` to a static writes into read-only memory.

A thread_shared object's fields sit at a different offset from a one-thread object's, so one compiled function cannot read both kinds.
owner_short.options:
A: one value, one place. The function that shares a value makes it where the sharing line needs it, and from that line the local is one of the owners. So views survive sharing, `thread_shared s` works after `s = Settings()`, and a static can be linked.

B: decide at the line (Rust's way). A view across the sharing line is refused, `thread_shared` goes only on a new value (E7017 kept), and a `weakref` to a static is refused.

C: A, but keep E7017. A value shared between threads must be created shared: `s = thread_shared Settings(port=8080)`.

method1_repair.open_risks:
1. The kind of a link place. A `weakref T` field may hold links made through one-thread names and links made through `thread_shared` names, which open differently (WK-12) and count differently (RC-4). This rule makes the kind known at every line that makes a link, because a value shared between threads is linked only through a `thread_shared` name. But the place's kind must be followed per place (P10's origins), or the opening must test the header. P01 and P10 should settle this, with this rule's E7015.

2. OBJ-1 decides a class family's weak count from every `weakref` "in the program", and that changes the family's field offsets. So it is already a whole-program fact across package edges today. It is not created here, and the new layout follows it unchanged. Flag it for the lead.

3. The two loads for an away-count operation through a base-class or `dyn` owner. Measure them on verdict 101's camera program before calling them negligible.

4. The move of a class object from elsewhere where the sharing line cannot take it: one allocation and one copy where the object reaches the function, on every path. An object C keeps then stops the program there, even on a path that never shares. That needs an object from elsewhere, given to C, shared on one path and used after the paths meet. The message names the sharing line.

5. The new summary fact (which parameters a function may link, and whether it keeps the link) is shared with P10's "which parameters it makes links from". Word it once.

6. In a function that may make a value `thread_shared`, a one-thread link to it is refused on every path, including a path that never shares it. That is an understandable limitation; the message names the sharing line.

7. A static's home thread follows P01's J8-10 (main, or the initialising thread under exports).

8. P09 owns header changes at a reload (item 2). P02's J5-05 (`thread_shared` in a manager) applies at the sharing line unchanged.

9. R3's readability reason (that a later line narrows what `s` may do) is the owner's to weigh. Option C exists for it.

10. An inferred "frame that never moves" (the engineering breaker's idea for generators) would accept a view into a frame held across `yield`. It is a separate language question and is not needed here.

11. Codes and messages are the lead's: E7017's narrowed meaning, and the new cases of E2020 and E7015.
